newsitem.title: MEXICO: OECD urges Mexico to boost spending, plan ahead.
newsitem.headline: OECD urges Mexico to boost spending, plan ahead.

text.p: Mexico must map out a clear strategy for the future and increase social spending to make up for some of the huge setbacks caused by its 1994-1995 economic crisis, the OECD said in a report on Thursday.

While praising the government for the speed with which it shook off Mexico's worst slump in decades, the Paris-based Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development said the crisis management of the last two years no longer sufficed.

It appeared to soften demands for the sort of rigorous fiscal austerity that international agencies have long urged on Mexico, and that critics say some of Mexico's U.S.-trained "technocrats" find hard to abandon.
"As immediate stabilization objectives are now largely met, it would be time to define a well-articulated medium-term strategy," the 169-page annual OECD report said.

The Paris-based OECD is a group of mostly wealthy nations that Mexico joined amid great fanfare in May 1994, seven months before its devaluation of the peso shook world markets and sent its GDP plummeting.

The main thrust of the OECD's recommendations was to build up infrastructure, education and worker training and ease poverty via basic nutrition and health services -- all areas chronically underfunded in Mexico that the government has only recently begun to tackle.

In addition, it said, the costs of dealing with the crisis -- bailing out the banking sector, paying off a huge international rescue package and reforming the pension and health systems -- needed to be clearly spelt out.

The government of President Ernesto Zedillo has sought to allay fears on Mexico's future by stressing that it will remain committed to balanced budgets. But that, the OECD said, "is too rough an indication".

Though it projected Mexico would achieve a growth rate of five percent in 1997, enough to restore the economy to pre- crisis levels of activity, it pointed to potential pitfalls that could waylay the recovery, such as the lingering weakness of the banking sector that almost collapsed in 1995.

The key to retaining investor confidence in Mexico during the uncertain period ahead lay in stating specific medium-term goals, including inflation targets beyond the next 12-month period and central bank policies to achieve them, the OECD said.
In an in-depth analysis of Mexico's labor market, it also laid out a long list of policy recommendations to help ease a situation in which half of the population lives in poverty.
The level of joblessness in Mexico is on paper lower than that of many OECD countries in Europe, running between two and five percent during most of the 1981-1994 period.

But the report pointed out that most Mexicans simply cannot afford to be out of work. There are no unemployment benefits, so dismissed workers must take to the streets as vendors, window washers or repairmen in times of crisis, or migrate to the countryside or the United States, the OECD said.
In the 1995 slump, when more than a million people lost their jobs, there was a surge of employment in the informal sector that the organization said had to be tackled.

Mexican wages are also notoriously fickle. In 1993, before the latest crisis, real wages remained below 1981 levels. The OECD said the ability of employers to cut wages meant they were prone to do that rather than fire staff.
To overhaul its labor market, the OECD urged Mexico to encourage more workers into the formal sector -- thus boosting tax collection -- and reform collective bargaining practices.
It also suggested carefully introducing some sort of inexpensive unemployment benefits scheme for times of crisis, suggesting Mexican workers could not take much more pain.
"As long as it is not permanent, emergency intervention of the type implemented in 1995-96 is clearly justified from a social point of view," the report said.
